title: Misplaced modifiers and parallel structure
blurb: Fix misplaced, dangling and limiting modifiers, and make lists, pairs, comparisons and correlative pairs parallel.
question: An applicant's essay says, “Hoping to get into the program, the essay was rewritten three times. I enjoy reading, volunteering, and to work with children.” What is wrong with each sentence, and how should it read?

teach.body: Formally, a modifier is a word, phrase or clause that describes another word, and it must sit next to that word, which must appear in the sentence. Parallel structure means that items joined in a series, a pair or a comparison share the same grammatical form. Plain English: a describing phrase sticks to its nearest neighbor, so put it beside the right one; and once a list starts a pattern (all -ing words, all to-verbs, all nouns), keep it.

rows.label: Problem
values: Target word is too far away

rows.label: Example
values: Served soup to patients in bowls
Walking in, the lights were bright

teach.caption: Fixed: “She served soup in bowls to the patients.” “Walking into the clinic, Ana noticed the bright lights.”

steps.label: Spot the opener
steps.sub: Walking in, / To pass the test, / After eating,

teach.caption: The subject right after an introductory phrase must be the one doing the action in that phrase. Switching to the passive voice does not fix it.

teach.note: Only, just, almost, nearly and even go directly before the word they limit. An item keys on placement only when the stem states the meaning.

teach.body: Joining words (and, or, but, than, as) are signals: whatever sits on one side must match what sits on the other. “She likes reading, hiking, and swimming” is parallel; “reading, hiking, and to swim” breaks the pattern. Check the last item of every list hardest, because the break usually hides there and sounds natural when you read fast.

rows.label: Correlative
values: not only fast but cheap too
not only fast but also cheap

teach.caption: Bracket each item the joining word links, name its form, then rewrite the odd one to match the others.

head: Pattern
Parallel example
rows: greeting visitors, answering phones, and filing charts
to listen, to explain, and to reassure
greeted visitors, answered phones, and filed charts
that she was ready and that she had studied

teach.body: Both...and, either...or, neither...nor and not only...but also come in pairs, and the words right after each half must match: “either on the website or at the front desk,” not “either check in on the website or at the front desk.” Keep the full pair (not only...but also). A comparison must also compare like with like: “Ana's score was higher than Jordan's” (score with score), not “higher than Jordan” (score with a person).

Nursing applicant Jasmine Brooks wrote: “Hoping to get into the program, the essay was rewritten three times. I enjoy reading, volunteering, and to work with children.” The opener dangles: an essay cannot hope. Fix: “Hoping to get into the program, I rewrote my essay three times.” The list mixes two -ing words with a to-verb, so the last item becomes working. Final: “I enjoy reading, volunteering, and working with children.”

teach.text: Dangling modifiers sound fine when you read fast, because your brain fills in the doer. On the HESI A2, always check the first noun after an introductory phrase: if it cannot do the action (lights cannot walk, an essay cannot hope), the modifier dangles. For lists, the odd item is usually the last one.

items: Place a modifier next to the word it describes; put only, just, almost and nearly right before the word they limit.
After an introductory phrase, the subject must be the doer of that phrase's action; passive voice does not fix it.
Items in a series, pair or comparison share one grammatical form; check the last item hardest.
Correlative pairs (both/and, either/or, neither/nor, not only/but also) take matching elements after each half.
Compare like with like: Ana's score with Jordan's, wait times with those at the other clinic.

summary: You can now spot and fix misplaced and dangling modifiers and place limiting words precisely. You can also make series, pairs, comparisons and correlative pairs parallel, and find the break that usually hides in the last item.

A.q: Which sentence is free of a dangling modifier?
options: Hurrying to the lab, Devon dropped the sample tray.
Hurrying to the lab, the sample tray fell to the floor.
Hurrying to the lab, the tray slipped from Devon's hands.
Hurrying to the lab, the samples were dropped by Devon.
A.why: Devon is the one hurrying, and he is the subject right after the introductory phrase.

whyNot.1: The tray becomes the subject, so the sentence says the tray was hurrying.
whyNot.2: The tray is still the subject; Devon appears as a possessive, not as the doer.
whyNot.3: The passive voice makes the samples the subject; Devon is not the doer after the comma.

A.q: Which sentence about an aide's tasks has parallel structure?
options: The aide's tasks are bathing patients, changing linens, and to restock supplies.
The aide's tasks are bathing patients, changing linens, and restocking supplies.
The aide's tasks are to bathe patients, changing linens, and restocking supplies.
The aide's tasks are bathing patients, to change linens, and restocking supplies.
A.why: All three items are -ing phrases: bathing, changing, restocking.

whyNot.0: The last item switches to a to-verb (to restock).
whyNot.2: The first item is a to-verb (to bathe) while the others use -ing.
whyNot.3: The middle item is a to-verb (to change) while the others use -ing.

A.q: Ray wants to say that he slept four hours and no more before the exam. Which sentence says this most clearly?
options: Only Ray slept four hours before the exam.
Ray slept four hours before the only exam.
Ray slept four hours before the exam only.
Ray slept only four hours before the exam.
A.why: Only sits directly before four hours, the amount it limits.

whyNot.0: Only before Ray means nobody else slept four hours.
whyNot.1: Only before exam suggests there was just one exam, which is a different meaning.
whyNot.2: Only at the end limits the time: he slept four hours before the exam and at no other time.

B.q: Which sentence about the nursing program uses the correlative pair correctly?
options: The program is not only affordable but also flexible.
The program not only is affordable but also flexible.
The program is not only affordable but also it is flexible.
The program is both affordable and it is flexible.
B.why: An adjective follows each half of the pair: not only affordable, but also flexible.

whyNot.1: A verb (is affordable) follows not only, but an adjective (flexible) follows but also.
whyNot.2: An adjective follows not only, but a clause (it is flexible) follows but also.
whyNot.3: An adjective follows both, but a clause (it is flexible) follows and.

B.q: The sticker has a smiley face on it. Which sentence places the modifier correctly?
options: The nurse gave a sticker to the boy with a smiley face.
With a smiley face, the nurse gave the boy a sticker.
The nurse gave the boy a sticker with a smiley face.
The nurse with a smiley face gave the boy a sticker.
B.why: “With a smiley face” sits right after sticker, the word it describes.

whyNot.0: The phrase now sits next to boy, so the boy seems to have the smiley face.
whyNot.1: The opening phrase attaches to the nurse, the subject after the comma.
whyNot.3: The phrase directly describes the nurse.

B.q: Which comparison about getting to class is written in parallel form?
options: Walking to class is healthier than to drive.
To walk to class is healthier than driving.
Walking to class is healthier than if you drive.
Walking to class is healthier than driving.
B.why: Both sides of than use an -ing form: walking ... driving.

whyNot.0: Walking (-ing) is compared with to drive (to-verb).
whyNot.1: To walk (to-verb) is compared with driving (-ing).
whyNot.2: Walking (-ing) is compared with a clause (if you drive).

C.q: Which revision corrects the dangling modifier in “To pass the HESI A2, careful study is required”?
options: To pass the HESI A2, careful study is required by students.
To pass the HESI A2, students need careful study.
To pass the HESI A2, it requires careful study.
To pass the HESI A2, a careful study plan is needed.
C.why: Students are the ones who will pass the HESI A2, and they are now the subject right after the opening phrase.

whyNot.0: Careful study is still the subject, so study seems to be passing the HESI A2.
whyNot.2: It has no clear antecedent and cannot pass a test.
whyNot.3: A study plan is now the subject, and a plan cannot pass the HESI A2.

C.q: Which sentence about weekend plans is NOT parallel?
options: The applicant was nervous, tired, and hungry.
She prefers studying at night to studying at dawn.
He likes to swim, to run, and biking on weekends.
We can meet in the library or at the cafe.
C.why: Two to-verbs (to swim, to run) are followed by an -ing word (biking), which breaks the pattern.

whyNot.1: Parallel: studying ... studying on both sides of the comparison.
whyNot.3: Parallel: two prepositional phrases joined by or.

C.q: Which sentence about two applicants makes a logical comparison?
options: Ana's score on the math section was higher than Jordan's.
Ana's score on the math section was higher than Jordan.
Ana's score on the math section was higher than Jordan scored.
Ana scored higher on the math section than Jordan's score.
C.why: Two things of the same kind are compared: Ana's score and Jordan's (score).

whyNot.1: This compares a score with a person, Jordan.
whyNot.2: This compares a score (a noun) with a clause (Jordan scored).
whyNot.3: This compares a person, Ana, with a score.

reteach.title: Magnets and matching uniforms
reteach.question: Picture every describing phrase as a small magnet, and every list as a team photo. What goes wrong when a magnet is next to the wrong thing, or when one player wears the wrong uniform?

blocks.h: Magnets stick to the nearest neighbor
blocks.body: Put the magnet “with a smiley face” next to boy and the boy gets the smiley face; put it next to sticker and the sticker does. A dangling modifier is a magnet with nothing to stick to: “After eating lunch, the shift started” has no person who ate, so the magnet grabs the shift.

In a list, every item is a team member. If two wear -ing uniforms (greeting, answering) and the third wears a to-verb uniform (to schedule), the third looks wrong in the photo. Change the odd one to match the team.

rows.label: Misplaced
values: the boy with a smiley face
a sticker with a smiley face

rows.label: Dangling
values: After lunch, Jo began her shift

blocks.text: The player out of uniform usually stands last in line, and a magnet near the start of a sentence grabs whatever noun comes right after the comma.

explain.body: Put each modifier beside the word it describes. Limiting words (only, just, almost, nearly, even) go directly before the word they limit, and moving them changes the meaning.

test.q: Carlos finished most of the charts but not all of them. Which sentence says this clearly?
options: Carlos almost finished all of the charts.
Carlos finished almost all of the charts.
Carlos finished all of the charts almost.
Almost Carlos finished all of the charts.
test.why: Almost sits directly before all, so it limits the number of charts: most, but not every one, were finished.

whyNot.0: Almost before finished limits the action, saying he came close to finishing rather than telling how many he finished.
whyNot.2: Almost at the end is misplaced and leaves the meaning unclear.
whyNot.3: Almost before Carlos limits Carlos, which makes no sense.

explain.body: An introductory phrase with no subject of its own borrows the subject after the comma. If that subject cannot do the action, the modifier dangles. Fix it by naming the doer as the subject.

rows.label: Example
values: After eating, Jo began her shift.

test.q: Which sentence contains a dangling modifier?
options: After finishing the shift, Rae drove home.
After Rae finished her long shift, she drove home.
After finishing the shift, Rae felt tired.
After finishing the shift, the drive felt long.
test.why: The drive is the subject after the comma, but a drive cannot finish a shift. The doer (Rae) is missing.

whyNot.0: Rae finished the shift and is the subject, so the modifier is attached correctly.
whyNot.1: The opener is a full clause with its own subject (Rae), so nothing dangles.
whyNot.2: Rae finished the shift and is the subject, so the modifier is attached correctly.

explain.body: Every item in a list takes the same form as the first: nouns with nouns, -ing with -ing, to-verbs with to-verbs.

test.q: Which choice correctly completes the sentence? “The nursing program values honesty, teamwork, and ___.”
options: being compassionate
to be compassionate
compassion
that you are compassionate
test.why: Honesty and teamwork are nouns, so the third item must be a noun: compassion.

whyNot.0: Being compassionate is an -ing phrase, not a noun like the others.
whyNot.1: To be compassionate is a to-verb phrase, not a noun.
whyNot.3: A clause does not match two single nouns.

explain.body: Both/and, either/or, neither/nor and not only/but also must be complete pairs, and each half must be followed by the same kind of element. Comparisons set like things side by side.

head: Pair
Parallel example
rows: not only for nurses but also for aides
neither on Monday nor on Tuesday
wait times here than those there

test.q: Which choice correctly completes the sentence? “The workshop is designed not only for new nurses ___.”
options: but experienced aides also
and also for experienced aides
but also experienced aides
but also for experienced aides
test.why: Not only is followed by “for new nurses,” so but also needs the same structure: “for experienced aides.”

whyNot.0: Drops for and splits but also, so the halves do not match.
whyNot.1: Not only must pair with but also, not and also.
whyNot.2: Missing for, so a phrase is matched with a bare noun.
